sections.title: How to Work Through the Projects

blocks.text:
The earlier Parts explained Redis one idea at a time. This Part puts the ideas together. You will build four small but complete services, each one a slice of ShopStream: a catalogue service with a hardened cache, a rate limiter, a flash-sale service that must never oversell, and a leaderboard with live notifications. Each project is small enough to finish in an evening and realistic enough to teach you the problems you will meet at work.

Every project follows the same shape, so you always know where you are:

1. **Goal and requirements**: what the service must do, stated so you can test it.
2. **Architecture and layout**: a sketch and the file tree.
3. **Build and run files**: `pom.xml` dependencies, `docker-compose.yml`, `application.yml`.
4. **The code**: the key classes in full, followed by "what to notice".
5. **Verify with redis-cli**: look at the keys your code created.
6. **Tests**: integration tests against a real Redis in a container (Testcontainers).
7. **Demo and extensions**: a behaviour or load demo, then ideas to push further.

### Common setup for all four projects

All four projects use Java 21, Maven, Spring Boot 4.1 and Spring Data Redis 4.1 with the default Lettuce client. You need a JDK 21, Maven 3.9+ and Docker. Each project is a separate Maven module with its own `pom.xml`; they share nothing except the conventions below, so you can build them in any order.

rows: `redis:8`, which includes the Bloom filter, JSON and Search commands without extra modules
`entity:id:field` with colons; every project documents its keys in a table
`StringRedisTemplate` for strings, counters and Lua; JSON is written by hand with the Boot-provided `JsonMapper`
`@SpringBootTest` plus a Redis container declared as a bean with `@ServiceConnection`
blocks.caption: Conventions shared by the projects.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text: Version numbers in the `pom.xml` listings are the ones the Spring Boot parent manages. Use the latest 4.1.x patch release of `spring-boot-starter-parent`; do not pin Spring Data Redis, Lettuce, Micrometer or Testcontainers yourself.

Two choices recur and are worth explaining once. First, we call Lua scripts through `DefaultRedisScript` with only string arguments. `StringRedisTemplate` serialises script arguments with its string serializer, so a `Long` argument would fail; always pass `String.valueOf(n)`. Second, our tests start a real Redis through Testcontainers rather than mocking `StringRedisTemplate`. A mock cannot tell you whether your Lua script, your key expiry or your Bloom filter command works, and those are the parts that break.

blocks.title: Tip
blocks.text: Type the code yourself the first time, at least for the core classes. The compile errors and the first failing test teach more than a pasted listing does. Compare with the listing afterwards.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
Each project is a vertical slice: HTTP endpoint, Redis data model, atomic logic, tests.

- Run Redis in Docker; run the service on your machine so you can use a debugger.
- Document every key you create; a service whose keys you cannot list is a service you cannot operate.
- Test against a real Redis; mock only the slow database.
- Pass only strings to scripts executed through `StringRedisTemplate`.

sections.title: Project A: A Production-Grade Catalogue Cache

blocks.text:
### Goal and requirements

ShopStream's catalog-service answers `GET /api/products/{id}` thousands of times per second, and the product database is slow (we will simulate 50 ms per lookup). The cache-aside pattern from the Patterns Part is the starting point. In this project we harden it against the four failures that bite real caches.

rows: Look in Redis first, load from the database on a miss, store the result
Base TTL 10 minutes plus or minus 20 percent, so keys loaded together do not expire together
A product that does not exist is remembered for 60 seconds as a marker value
Ids that were never created are rejected before they reach the cache or the database
When a hot key expires, only one request reloads it; the rest wait briefly and read the result
Counters for hit, miss, negative and Bloom rejections, and a counter of database loads
blocks.caption: Requirements.

blocks.text:
The last metric is the one that proves the work. If 200 concurrent requests for a cold key cause exactly one database load, the design works.

### Architecture

The Bloom filter has one-sided error: it can say "maybe present" for an id that does not exist (a false positive), but it never says "absent" for an id that was added. That is exactly the property we need to shield the database from random ids, and the negative cache covers the false positives.

### Project layout

Gotcha
blocks.text: Spring Boot 4 split its auto-configuration into smaller modules and renamed some starters (the web starter is now `spring-boot-starter-webmvc`, with a matching `spring-boot-starter-webmvc-test`). If a tutorial written for Boot 3 does not compile, check starter names and test-annotation packages first. The listings in this Part avoid MockMvc-style test slices so they depend on as little of that as possible.

blocks.code:
services:
  redis:
    image: redis:8
    container_name: shopstream-redis
    ports:
      - "6379:6379"
    command: ["redis-server", "--appendonly", "no", "--maxmemory", "256mb",

    healthcheck:

blocks.title: docker-compose.yml

blocks.text: We set `maxmemory` and an eviction policy because a cache without a memory limit is not a cache, it is a slow memory leak. `allkeys-lru` is the usual choice for a pure cache. Note it can also evict the Bloom filter and lock keys; the extension ideas at the end of the chapter show how to cope.

catalog:
  ttl: 10m
  ttl-jitter: 0.2
  negative-ttl: 60s
  lock-ttl: 5s

blocks.text: ### The domain and the slow database

blocks.title: Product.java
ProductRepository.java
SlowProductRepository.java
CatalogProperties.java

blocks.text:
### The Bloom filter and the lock

Both helpers are thin wrappers over commands run through Lua scripts. Going through `execute(RedisScript, ...)` gives us a typed result (`Long`) without touching low-level connection APIs. The Bloom filter commands (`BF.RESERVE`, `BF.ADD`, `BF.EXISTS`) are built into Redis 8.

blocks.title: BloomFilter.java
Watch out
blocks.text: If the Bloom key does not exist (for example it was evicted, or you flushed the database), `BF.EXISTS` returns 0 for everything and your service would answer 404 for every product. The startup runner below rebuilds the filter, but in production you also want an alert on `EXISTS bf:product:ids` and a way to rebuild it without a restart. Either exclude the key from eviction by using a `volatile-*` policy (it has no TTL) or run the filter on a Redis that never evicts.

blocks.title: SingleFlightLock.java

blocks.text:
What to notice: `setIfAbsent(key, value, Duration)` sends a single `SET key value NX PX ms` command, so the lock and its expiry are set atomically. The lock has a TTL (5 seconds) so a crashed instance cannot block a key forever, and the release script checks the token so a slow request cannot delete a lock that has since passed to someone else. This is the single-key lock from the distributed locking chapter, deliberately kept simple: here a lost or expired lock only means one extra database read, not corrupted data.

### The cache layer

`ProductCache` knows how products are stored: as JSON text under `product:{id}`, with a short marker for "this product does not exist". It returns a three-state result, so the caller can tell "not cached" from "cached as absent".

blocks.title: ProductCache.java
Note
blocks.text: Jackson 3 lives in the `tools.jackson` packages, and its exceptions are unchecked, which is why `readValue` needs no `throws` clause. Spring Boot 4 auto-configures a `JsonMapper` bean, so we simply inject it. Java records are supported by Jackson without extra annotations.

Jitter deserves a number. With a fixed 600-second TTL, 10,000 products loaded in the same minute would all expire in the same minute, and the database would see a wave of 10,000 loads. With plus or minus 20 percent the expiry times spread over a 240-second window (480 to 720 seconds), which flattens the wave to roughly 40 loads per second on average. The exact figures are illustrative; the idea is to turn a spike into a slope.

### The service: putting the defences in order

The order of the checks matters: cheapest and most selective first.

blocks.title: CatalogService.java
CatalogMetrics.java

blocks.text:
What to notice in `CatalogService`:

- **Bloom first.** One cheap `BF.EXISTS` round trip protects the cache and database from ids that were never valid.
- **Double-check after winning the lock.** Between our cache miss and our lock acquisition another request may have finished loading. Without this second `get`, every request that queued behind the first would reload the same row one after another.
- **Waiters poll, they do not block on the lock.** A waiter checks the cache every 20 ms for up to `wait-max`. If the owner is slow or dead, the waiter falls back to loading itself, so the lock can only make things faster, never wedge a request.
- **Write path deletes, it does not update.** After `save` we delete the cached entry and let the next read repopulate it. This is simpler than writing the new value and avoids storing a value computed from stale data.
- `Timer.record(Supplier)` counts every database load, and its `count` statistic is our proof of single-flight behaviour.

blocks.title: Gotcha
blocks.text: Delete-after-write still has a tiny race: a reader that loaded the old row just before the write can put the old value back just after your delete. The jittered TTL bounds the damage (the stale entry expires), and for most catalogues that is acceptable. If it is not, version the entries or use short TTLs for frequently edited products.
### The HTTP layer and startup warm-up

blocks.title: ProductController.java
CatalogApplication.java

blocks.text:
The filter is sized for 100,000 ids at a 1 percent false-positive rate. If more ids are added later, the filter auto-scales by creating sub-filters (the default unless `NONSCALING` is passed), at the cost of a somewhat higher combined error rate and more memory.

### Verify with redis-cli

Start Redis with `docker compose up -d`, start the service with `mvn spring-boot:run`, then:

blocks.code:
$ curl -s localhost:8080/api/products/p-42
{"id":"p-42","name":"Product 42","price":1.26,"stock":100}
$ curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" localhost:8080/api/products/zzz-unknown
404
$ docker exec -it shopstream-redis redis-cli
127.0.0.1:6379> GET product:p-42
"{\"id\":\"p-42\",\"name\":\"Product 42\",\"price\":1.26,\"stock\":100}"
127.0.0.1:6379> TTL product:p-42
(integer) 541
127.0.0.1:6379> BF.EXISTS bf:product:ids p-42
(integer) 1
127.0.0.1:6379> BF.EXISTS bf:product:ids zzz-unknown
(integer) 0
127.0.0.1:6379> EXISTS product:zzz-unknown
(integer) 0
blocks.title: Watch the cache fill and the negative cache work

blocks.text: The unknown id left no trace: the Bloom filter rejected it, so there is no `product:zzz-unknown` key and no database load. Now simulate a deleted product, which is in the filter but not in the table. Remove it from the repository (or use a false-positive id) and request it twice; the second request is answered from the marker:

### Tests with Testcontainers

The test configuration declares the Redis container as a Spring bean. Spring Boot's `@ServiceConnection` then points `spring.data.redis.host` and `port` at the mapped container port automatically. Because `GenericContainer` does not reveal which service it runs, we give the hint with `name = "redis"`.

blocks.title: RedisTestConfig.java
CatalogServiceIT.java
Watch out
blocks.text: The stampede test is only meaningful if the database call is slower than the time it takes the threads to start, which is why the test property sets `catalog.db-latency-ms=100`. If you set it to zero, the test passes even without the lock because the first load finishes before the others miss. A test that cannot fail is not a test; break `loadOnce` on purpose (skip the lock) and confirm the test goes red.

### Demo: watch the database load counter

With the service running, fire 200 requests with 50 in parallel at a cold key, then read the counter:

blocks.code:
$ docker exec shopstream-redis redis-cli DEL product:p-500
(integer) 1
$ seq 1 200 | xargs -P 50 -I{} curl -s -o /dev/null localhost:8080/api/products/p-500
$ curl -s localhost:8080/actuator/metrics/catalog.db.loads | grep -o '"COUNT","value":[0-9.]*'
"COUNT","value":1.0
$ curl -s "localhost:8080/actuator/metrics/catalog.cache?tag=result:hit" | grep -o '"value":[0-9.]*'
"value":199.0
blocks.title: Single-flight under load

blocks.text: The exact split between hits and misses varies from run to run (a few early requests may be counted as misses while they wait); the number to watch is the single database load. Repeat the experiment after commenting out the lock in `loadOnce` and the counter will jump to the number of requests that arrived in the first 50 ms.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: How do you protect a database from a cache stampede, and from cache penetration? A stampede is many concurrent misses on one hot key (usually just after it expires); protect with single-flight loading (a short Redis lock or an in-process lock so one request reloads), TTL jitter so keys do not expire together, and optionally serving slightly stale data while one request refreshes. Penetration is repeated lookups for keys that do not exist; protect with negative caching (short-TTL marker), a Bloom filter of valid ids, and input validation.

### Extension ideas

- **Stale-while-revalidate.** Store a soft expiry inside the JSON and keep the Redis TTL longer. Serve the stale value immediately and let one request refresh in the background.
- **Two-level cache.** Add a small in-JVM Caffeine cache in front of Redis with a 5 second TTL, and compare latency. Then add client-side caching invalidation from the Redis chapter on tracking.
- **Warm the hot set.** On start, preload the top 500 products from the leaderboard of most viewed items.
- **Measure.** Add a `redis-benchmark` style load with 95 percent reads on 100 hot ids and chart p99 latency with and without jitter and single-flight.
- **Survive eviction.** Move the Bloom filter to its own Redis instance with `noeviction`, or rebuild it when `BF.EXISTS` on a known id returns 0.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
What this project proves:

- Cache-aside needs more than get/set: jittered TTLs, negative caching and single-flight loading each close a specific failure.
- A Bloom filter answers "definitely not here" for almost no memory and no database load.
- A lock used to save work can be short and lossy; a lost lock costs a duplicate read, so wait with a bounded timeout and fall back.
- Count database loads; that metric is the proof the cache does its job.
- Test with a slow fake database and a real Redis; both are needed to see stampedes.

sections.title: Project B: An API Rate Limiter Service

blocks.text:
### Goal and requirements

ShopStream's gateway must stop one noisy client from starving everyone else. Customers who pay get a larger allowance than anonymous visitors. You will build a rate limiter as a Spring MVC interceptor backed by one Lua script, so that the check-and-update is atomic no matter how many gateway instances run.

rows: Token bucket: a bucket holds up to `capacity` tokens, refills at `refill` tokens per second, and each request spends `cost` tokens
Read, refill, spend and write happen in one Lua script; two instances can never both spend the last token
Each API key maps to a plan (`anonymous`, `free`, `pro`) with its own capacity and refill rate
An expensive route such as search can cost several tokens
`429 Too Many Requests` with `Retry-After`, plus `X-RateLimit-Limit` and `X-RateLimit-Remaining` on every response
If Redis is unreachable the limiter fails open (requests pass) and counts the event
The script uses the Redis `TIME` command, so application servers with skewed clocks do not matter
blocks.caption: Requirements.

blocks.text:
### Why a token bucket

The Patterns Part compared three algorithms. As a reminder of the trade-offs that led to this choice:

rows: A client can send 2× the limit across a window boundary
One sorted-set member per request; memory grows with the limit
Allows controlled bursts, two numbers of state per client
Slightly harder to explain; needs the script below
blocks.caption: Algorithms at a glance.

blocks.text: The bucket is a hash with two fields: `tokens` (a number that may be fractional) and `ts` (the millisecond time of the last update). On each request the script computes how many tokens have accumulated since `ts`, caps the total at `capacity`, tries to spend `cost`, and writes the new state back. Idle clients cost nothing: the hash gets a TTL slightly longer than the time needed to refill a full bucket, after which a fresh client is indistinguishable from a forgotten one.

blocks.code:
capacity = 10, refill = 5 tokens/s, cost = 1

time    0.0s   0.2s   0.4s   ...  1.0s        2.0s
tokens  10 ──► 9 ──► 8 ──► ... ► (burst of 10 sent, bucket empty)
                                   0 ──► +5 per second ──► steady 5 req/s
11th request at 0.0s → denied, Retry-After = ceil((1 - 0) / 5) = 1 s (rounded up)

blocks.text: ### Project layout

blocks.code:
rate-limiter/
  ├── pom.xml                      (same dependencies as Project A)
  ├── docker-compose.yml           (same Redis service as Project A)
  └── src
      ├── main
      │   ├── java/com/shopstream/ratelimit
      │   │   ├── RateLimiterApplication.java
      │   │   ├── RateLimitProperties.java
      │   │   ├── TokenBucketLimiter.java
      │   │   ├── RateLimitInterceptor.java
      │   │   ├── WebConfig.java
      │   │   └── DemoController.java
      │   └── resources
      │       ├── application.yml
      │       └── scripts/token_bucket.lua
      └── test/java/com/shopstream/ratelimit
          ├── RedisTestConfig.java
          └── RateLimiterIT.java

Thepom.xmlneedsspring-boot-starter-webmvc,spring-boot-starter-data-redis,

blocks.text:
`spring-boot-starter-actuator`, and for tests `spring-boot-starter-test` and `spring-boot-testcontainers`, exactly as in Project A. The `docker-compose.yml` can be reused unchanged; for a rate limiter you may prefer `--maxmemory-policy volatile-ttl`, because every bucket key has a TTL.

### Configuration

The limits are data, not code, so they live in `application.yml` and bind to a record.

blocks.code:
spring:
  application:
    name: rate-limiter
  data:
    redis:
      host: localhost
      port: 6379
      timeout: 200ms

ratelimit:
  fail-open: true
  plans:
    anonymous: { capacity: 10,  refill-per-second: 2 }
    free:      { capacity: 30,  refill-per-second: 10 }
    pro:       { capacity: 200, refill-per-second: 100 }
  keys:
    demo-free: free
    demo-pro: pro
  route-costs:
    "/api/search": 5

management:
  endpoints:
    web:
      exposure:
        include: health,metrics
blocks.title: application.yml
Note
blocks.text: The Redis `timeout: 200ms` is deliberate. A rate limiter is on the hot path of every request; if Redis stalls, you want the call to fail within a fraction of your request budget and trigger the fail-open policy, not hang for the default of one minute.

blocks.title: RateLimitProperties.java

blocks.text:
### The Lua script

The whole algorithm is one script. Read it top to bottom; there is no branching you cannot follow.

blocks.code:
-- KEYS[1] = bucket key
-- ARGV[1] = capacity (tokens)
-- ARGV[2] = refill rate (tokens per second)
-- ARGV[3] = cost of this request (tokens)
-- Returns { allowed (1/0), remaining tokens (floored), retry-after ms, ms until full }
local capacity = tonumber(ARGV[1])
local refill   = tonumber(ARGV[2])
local cost     = tonumber(ARGV[3])

local t   = redis.call('TIME')
local now = t[1] * 1000 + math.floor(t[2] / 1000)      -- milliseconds

local data   = redis.call('HMGET', KEYS[1], 'tokens', 'ts')
local tokens = tonumber(data[1])
local ts     = tonumber(data[2])
if tokens == nil then
  tokens = capacity
  ts = now
end

local elapsed = math.max(0, now - ts)
tokens = math.min(capacity, tokens + elapsed * refill / 1000)

local allowed = 0
local retry = 0
if tokens >= cost then
  tokens = tokens - cost
  allowed = 1
else
  retry = math.ceil((cost - tokens) * 1000 / refill)
end

redis.call('HSET', KEYS[1], 'tokens', tokens, 'ts', now)
local fullMs = math.ceil((capacity - tokens) * 1000 / refill)
redis.call('PEXPIRE', KEYS[1], math.ceil(capacity * 1000 / refill) + 1000)

return { allowed, math.floor(tokens), retry, fullMs }
blocks.title: scripts/token_bucket.lua

blocks.text:
What to notice:

- `TIME` **instead of the client clock.** Every application server shares Redis's single clock, so skewed server clocks cannot give one instance extra tokens. Since Redis 5, scripts are replicated by their effects (the resulting writes), so calling `TIME` in a script is safe.
- **State is written even when the request is denied.** Updating `ts` on a denial is correct because the refill has been accounted into `tokens`; skipping the write would make the next call recompute the same refill, which is also correct but wastes the TTL refresh.
- **Floating point stays inside the script.** Lua numbers are doubles. A Lua number returned to the client is truncated to an integer, which is why we return `math.floor` values and let Java deal with whole numbers.
- **One key, so no cluster problem.** Everything touches `KEYS[1]` only. In Redis Cluster that is required: a script may only touch keys that live in one slot, and it must declare them in `KEYS`.
- **Self-cleaning.** The `PEXPIRE` is slightly longer than the time to refill from empty. When it fires, the client's state is gone and the next request starts with a full bucket, which is exactly what the maths would have given.

### The limiter component

blocks.title: TokenBucketLimiter.java

blocks.text:
`DefaultRedisScript` computes the script's SHA-1 once. Spring Data Redis sends `EVALSHA` and, if the server answers with `NOSCRIPT` (after a restart or `SCRIPT FLUSH`), transparently falls back to `EVAL` and the server caches the script again. You never manage the SHA yourself.

### The interceptor

A `HandlerInterceptor` runs before the controller and sees the request and response, which is exactly the right place for a limiter that must add headers. A servlet `Filter` would also work and runs earlier (before Spring MVC mapping), which matters if you want to protect static resources too.

blocks.title: RateLimitInterceptor.java
WebConfig.java
DemoController.java
RateLimiterApplication.java

blocks.text:
What to notice in the interceptor:

- **Identity before limiting.** An unknown API key is a `401`, not a free pass to the anonymous plan; otherwise attackers could rotate fake keys to get fresh buckets.
- **Fail-open versus fail-closed is a business decision.** For a public catalogue, blocking all traffic because the limiter is down is worse than briefly having no limit. For a login or payment endpoint you may choose fail-closed. The code makes it one property.
- **Headers on every response,** `Retry-After` **only on** `429`**.** Clients can pace themselves before they are blocked. `Retry-After` is rounded up to whole seconds, as the HTTP header requires.
- **The route cost is looked up by exact URI.** For real routes with path variables, use the matched pattern from the request attribute instead; see the extensions.

blocks.title: Watch out
blocks.text: `req.getRemoteAddr()` behind a load balancer or gateway is the balancer's address, so every anonymous user would share one bucket. Behind a trusted proxy, read `X-Forwarded-For` (or configure `server.forward-headers-strategy`), and never trust that header from the open internet, where clients can forge it.

### Verify with redis-cli

Start Redis and the service, then spend the anonymous bucket (capacity 10) quickly:

blocks.code:
$ for i in $(seq 1 12); do \
    curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code} " localhost:8080/api/ping; done; echo
200 200 200 200 200 200 200 200 200 200 429 429
$ curl -si localhost:8080/api/ping | head -8
HTTP/1.1 429
X-RateLimit-Limit: 10
X-RateLimit-Remaining: 0
Retry-After: 1
Content-Type: application/json

{"error":"rate_limited","retryAfterMs":388}
blocks.title: Burst, then denial
Note
blocks.text: `KEYS` is fine on an empty development instance and is the quickest way to look; on a busy server use `SCAN 0 MATCH` `rl:* COUNT 100` instead. The IPv6 loopback address in the key (`0:0:0:0:0:0:0:1`) is what you see when `curl` connects to `localhost` over IPv6; the exact values in your output will differ.
Now try the paid plan and the weighted route:

blocks.code:
$ curl -s -H "X-API-Key: demo-pro" -o /dev/null -D - localhost:8080/api/search | grep X-Rate
X-RateLimit-Limit: 200
X-RateLimit-Remaining: 195
$ curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" -H "X-API-Key: wrong" localhost:8080/api/ping
401
blocks.title: Plans and weights

blocks.text:
The search call cost 5 tokens, so 200 became 195.

### Tests

We reuse the same `RedisTestConfig` pattern as Project A (a `GenericContainer<>("redis:8")` bean with `@ServiceConnection(name = "redis")`). The tests set tiny plans so they run in milliseconds. To call the running server we use the JDK `HttpClient` and the `local.server.port` property, which keeps the test independent of Spring Boot 4's reorganised web-test packages.

blocks.title: RateLimiterIT.java

blocks.text:
The third test is the important one. It fires 200 calls from 32 threads at a bucket of 5 tokens and asserts that exactly 5 were allowed. If you replace the Lua script with a Java read-modify-write (`HGET`, compute, `HSET`), this test will fail intermittently and show you the race that the script prevents.

### Demo: two clients, one noisy

Run two terminals. In the first, hammer the API as an anonymous client; in the second, use the pro key and watch it keep succeeding:

blocks.code:
$ seq 1 100 | xargs -P 10 -I{} curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" localhost:8080/api/ping \
    | sort | uniq -c
     11 200
     89 429
$ curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" -H "X-API-Key: demo-pro" localhost:8080/api/ping
200
$ curl -s "localhost:8080/actuator/metrics/ratelimit.requests?tag=result:denied" \
    | grep -o '"value":[0-9.]*'
"value":89.0
blocks.title: Isolation between clients

blocks.text: The anonymous count is 11 rather than 10 because a fraction of a token refills while the 100 requests are being sent. Your exact numbers will vary slightly.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: Why implement a rate limiter in a Lua script instead of Java code with GET and SET? Read-modify-write across the network is a race: two app servers read the same token count and both spend the last token. Redis runs a script as one atomic unit on its single command thread, so no other command interleaves between the read and the write. The alternative is optimistic locking with `WATCH`/`MULTI` and retries, which is slower under contention. A script also saves round trips: one instead of two or three.

blocks.title: Real world
blocks.text: Production limiters usually sit in the API gateway or a sidecar, not inside every service, and often combine a coarse per-IP limit at the edge with finer per-key limits behind it. The Redis part is almost always some variant of this script. The cost to watch is one Redis round trip (typically well under a millisecond on a local network) added to every request; keep Redis in the same zone as the gateway.

### Extension ideas

- **Per-route buckets.** Use the matched pattern (`HandlerMapping.BEST_MATCHING_PATTERN_ATTRIBUTE`) in the key, giving `rl:{identity}:{route}`, so a busy route cannot exhaust a quiet one.
- **Local fallback.** When Redis is down, fall back to a small in-process Guava or Caffeine-based limiter rather than no limit at all.
- **Sliding window variant.** Implement the sorted-set sliding window log as a second script and compare memory with `MEMORY USAGE` for 1,000 clients.
- **Dynamic plans.** Store plans in a Redis hash (`plan:{name}`) so an operator can change limits without a deploy.
- **Cluster test.** Run the tests against a three-node Redis Cluster and confirm all keys of one identity still live in one slot (they do, since each script touches one key).

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
What this project proves:

- A token bucket needs two numbers of state per client and one atomic script; Lua gives you atomicity without locks.
- Use the Redis `TIME` command for time arithmetic inside the script; do not trust application clocks.
- Decide the failure policy (fail open or closed) explicitly and give Redis a short client timeout.
- Give clients the information to behave: `Retry-After` and remaining-count headers.
- Prove atomicity with a concurrency test that would fail for a non-atomic implementation.

sections.title: Project C: A Flash-Sale Service That Never Oversells

blocks.text:
### Goal and requirements

At 12:00 sharp ShopStream drops 100 limited sneakers at half price, and 20,000 people click at once. Three things must hold, even with several service instances and a worker that may crash mid-job:

1. **Never oversell.** Exactly 100 units can be reserved, no matter how many requests race.
2. **Holds expire.** A shopper who reserves a pair has two minutes to pay; if they do not, the pair goes back on sale.
3. **Orders are processed exactly once in effect.** Confirmed reservations become order events on a Redis stream, consumed by a worker in a consumer group that survives crashes and redelivery.

rows: One Lua script (`reserve.lua`) decides: sold out, already bought, or reserved
A set `buyers:{sku}` checked and updated in the same script
Sorted set `resvexp:{sku}` scored by deadline in milliseconds, plus a hash with the details
A scheduled reaper finds due reservations; `release.lua` claims each one atomically and restores stock
`confirm.lua` claims the reservation with `ZREM`; whoever removes it wins, a retry gets "already confirmed"
`Idempotency-Key` header: replaying a request returns the first answer and does not spend stock twice
`confirm.lua` appends to `stream:orders`; a worker reads it as a member of group `fulfilment`, then `XACK`s
blocks.caption: Requirements.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text: In key names below, `{sku}` and `{id}` are placeholders, not Redis Cluster hash tags. This project is written for a single Redis (or primary with replicas), where scripts may touch any keys. To run it on Redis Cluster you would put a hash tag around the SKU in every key a script touches (for example `stock:{sku}`, literally with braces) so they share a slot, and send `XADD` from Java instead of from the script. The Scaling Part explains why.

### Why a script, not WATCH or a lock

There are three ways to decrement stock safely. A plain `DECR` and a check afterwards oversells briefly (the counter goes negative, and other requests see it). `WATCH` with `MULTI`/`EXEC` is correct but retries under contention, and a flash sale is pure contention: with 1,000 competing clients most `EXEC` calls fail and retry. A distributed lock works but serialises requests through an extra round trip each. A Lua script runs as one atomic step on Redis's single command thread: no retries, no lock, one round trip. A single Redis instance can run a very large number of such tiny scripts per second; in practice the network and the web tier usually saturate first, but measure your own setup with `redis-benchmark` or a load test.

### Architecture

blocks.code:
clients ──► SaleController ──► ReservationService ──────────► Redis
                                  │  reserve.lua   stock:{sku}        (string, integer)
                                  │                buyers:{sku}       (set of user ids)
                                  │                resvexp:{sku}      (zset id → deadline ms)
                                  │                resv:{sku}:{id}    (hash user, qty, status)
                                  │                idem:{sku}:{key}   (string → reservation id)
                                  │  confirm.lua ──► stream:orders ─────────────────┐
                                  │                                                 ▼
ExpiryReaper (1 s) ── release.lua              OrderWorker (group "fulfilment")
  (returns stock)                                └► OrderStore (idempotent put) + XACK

blocks.text: The reservation lifecycle is a tiny state machine. The sorted set is the arbiter: a reservation is "live" exactly while its id is in `resvexp:{sku}`. Both `confirm.lua` and `release.lua` try to `ZREM` the id first; Redis runs scripts one at a time, so exactly one of them succeeds. That removes the classic race between "shopper pays at 1:59" and "reaper expires at 2:00".

blocks.code:
reserve.lua                   confirm.lua (ZREM wins)
(none) ───────────────► RESERVED ───────────────────────────► PAID ──► stream:orders
                           │
                           │ release.lua (ZREM wins, deadline passed)
                           ▼
                        EXPIRED   (stock returned, shopper may try again)

blocks.text: ### Project layout

blocks.code:
flash-sale/
├── pom.xml                          (same dependencies as Project A, web + data-redis + test)
├── docker-compose.yml               (same Redis service)
└── src

Remember that even with the AOF on `everysec` you can lose about a second of writes in a crash, so for money-adjacent state the order of record should still be your database, fed from the stream.

blocks.code:
spring:
  application:
    name: flash-sale
  data:
    redis:
      host: localhost
      port: 6379

sale:
  hold: 2m

blocks.title: application.yml
SaleProperties.java

blocks.text:
### The three Lua scripts

`reserve.lua` is the heart of the project. Read it as a decision list: first match wins.

blocks.code:
-- KEYS: 1 stock, 2 buyers, 3 expiry zset, 4 reservation hash, 5 idempotency key
-- ARGV: 1 reservation id, 2 user id, 3 quantity, 4 hold time in ms
-- Returns { code, reservationId }
--   1 reserved | 3 duplicate request (replayed) | -1 already bought | -2 sold out | -3 no such sale
local previous = redis.call('GET', KEYS[5])
if previous then
  return { 3, previous }
end

local stock = redis.call('GET', KEYS[1])
if not stock then
  return { -3, '' }
end
if redis.call('SISMEMBER', KEYS[2], ARGV[2]) == 1 then
  return { -1, '' }
end
local qty = tonumber(ARGV[3])
if tonumber(stock) < qty then
  return { -2, '' }
end

local t = redis.call('TIME')
local now = t[1] * 1000 + math.floor(t[2] / 1000)

redis.call('DECRBY', KEYS[1], qty)
redis.call('SADD', KEYS[2], ARGV[2])
redis.call('ZADD', KEYS[3], now + tonumber(ARGV[4]), ARGV[1])
redis.call('HSET', KEYS[4], 'user', ARGV[2], 'qty', ARGV[3], 'status', 'RESERVED')
redis.call('EXPIRE', KEYS[4], 86400)
redis.call('SET', KEYS[5], ARGV[1], 'EX', 86400)
return { 1, ARGV[1] }
blocks.title: scripts/reserve.lua

blocks.code:
-- KEYS: 1 expiry zset, 2 reservation hash, 3 orders stream
-- ARGV: 1 reservation id, 2 sku
-- Returns 1 confirmed | 2 already confirmed | 0 expired or unknown
local deadline = redis.call('ZSCORE', KEYS[1], ARGV[1])
if not deadline then
  if redis.call('HGET', KEYS[2], 'status') == 'PAID' then
    return 2
  end
  return 0
end
local t = redis.call('TIME')
local now = t[1] * 1000 + math.floor(t[2] / 1000)
if tonumber(deadline) < now then
  return 0                      -- too late; the reaper will give the stock back
end

redis.call('ZREM', KEYS[1], ARGV[1])
local f = redis.call('HMGET', KEYS[2], 'user', 'qty')
redis.call('HSET', KEYS[2], 'status', 'PAID')
redis.call('XADD', KEYS[3], '*', 'orderId', ARGV[1], 'sku', ARGV[2], 'user', f[1], 'qty', f[2])
return 1
blocks.title: scripts/confirm.lua

blocks.code:
-- KEYS: 1 stock, 2 buyers, 3 expiry zset, 4 reservation hash
-- ARGV: 1 reservation id
-- Returns 1 if this call returned the stock, 0 if it was not due or someone else won
local deadline = redis.call('ZSCORE', KEYS[3], ARGV[1])
if not deadline then
  return 0
end
local t = redis.call('TIME')
local now = t[1] * 1000 + math.floor(t[2] / 1000)
if tonumber(deadline) > now then
  return 0
end

redis.call('ZREM', KEYS[3], ARGV[1])
local f = redis.call('HMGET', KEYS[4], 'user', 'qty')
redis.call('INCRBY', KEYS[1], f[2])
redis.call('SREM', KEYS[2], f[1])
redis.call('HSET', KEYS[4], 'status', 'EXPIRED')
return 1
blocks.title: scripts/release.lua

blocks.text:
What to notice:

- **Everything in** `reserve.lua` **is decided before anything is written.** All checks run first, then the five writes; there is no early return after a partial write, so the script never leaves half-applied state. (Redis scripts are atomic in the sense that nothing else runs in between, but they are not rolled back if a later command errors, so design them check-then-write.)
- `confirm.lua` **re-checks the deadline.** Between the reaper's runs, an overdue reservation still sits in the sorted set. Checking the time inside the script means a payment at second 121 is refused even if the reaper has not noticed yet.
- **Idempotency is part of the same script.** The first thing `reserve.lua` does is look up the replay key. Doing that in Java before the script would leave a window where two identical requests both pass the check.
- **Quantities are strings in the hash.** `HMGET` returns strings; `INCRBY` accepts a numeric string. Redis would reject a value that is not an integer, which would abort the script, so validate `qty` in Java first.
- **Long-running scripts block everything.** These run in microseconds. Never put a loop over thousands of reservations into one script; the reaper processes ids one script call at a time for this reason.

### The reservation service

blocks.title: ReservationService.java
ExpiryReaper.java

blocks.text:
What to notice: the reaper is safe to run on every instance at once. If two instances pick the same expired reservation, `release.lua` lets only one succeed (`ZREM` wins). That is the same trick as the lock-free claims in the job-queue pattern, and it means you do not need leader election. The `horizon` is slightly ahead of local time only to fetch candidates; the script is the authority on whether the deadline has passed.

### The controller

blocks.title: SaleController.java

blocks.text:
Why `409 Conflict` for sold out and `410 Gone` for an expired hold? They are conventions, not rules. The point is that a client can tell "you lost the race" (stop, show the sold-out page) from "your hold lapsed" (offer to try again) without parsing messages.

### The order pipeline: stream and consumer group

`confirm.lua` appends one entry per paid reservation to `stream:orders`. The worker is a member of consumer group `fulfilment`. A stream gives you what a plain list cannot: entries stay after delivery, each consumer has a list of delivered-but-unacknowledged entries (the pending entries list, PEL), and a crashed worker's work can be picked up again.

blocks.title: OrderStore.java
OrderWorker.java

blocks.text:
What to notice in the worker:

- **Pending first, then new.** Reading offset `0` returns this consumer's own unacknowledged entries; reading `>` returns entries never delivered to anyone. If the process dies between saving an order and `XACK`, the entry is delivered again on restart. Because the consumer name is random in this demo, a restarted worker is a new consumer and would not see the old PEL; in production use a stable name (the pod name) or run `XAUTOCLAIM` to adopt entries idle for too long. See the extensions.
- **Processing is idempotent.** `putIfAbsent` on the order id means a redelivered entry cannot create a second order. Streams give you at-least-once delivery; idempotent handlers turn that into exactly-once effect.
- **Acknowledge only after the work.** `XACK` follows the save. Reversing the order would lose the order on a crash between the two.
- `createGroup` **creates the stream if needed.** Spring Data Redis issues `XGROUP CREATE` with `MKSTREAM`, so starting the worker before any sale works. A restart finds the group already present and the server answers `BUSYGROUP`, which we tolerate.

blocks.title: Gotcha
blocks.text: A consumer group that nobody reads is not free: unacknowledged entries stay in the PEL and the stream itself keeps growing. Trim the stream (`XTRIM`, or `XADD ... MAXLEN ~`) once you are sure every group has acknowledged. Since Redis 8.2 you can also use `XACKDEL` and the `ACKED` option to delete entries only once all groups have acknowledged them; check the command pages for exact syntax before relying on it.

blocks.title: FlashSaleApplication.java

blocks.text:
### Verify with redis-cli

Open a sale of three units, reserve and confirm one, and look at the state:

blocks.code:
$ curl -s -X POST "localhost:8080/api/sales/sneaker-1?stock=3"
{"sku":"sneaker-1","stock":3}
$ curl -s -X POST localhost:8080/api/sales/sneaker-1/reservations \
    -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"userId":"u1","qty":1}'
{"reservationId":"c0a8f1de-5d3c-4b6e-9a53-7a4e2c1b9f10"}
127.0.0.1:6379> GET stock:sneaker-1
"2"
127.0.0.1:6379> SMEMBERS buyers:sneaker-1
1) "u1"
127.0.0.1:6379> ZRANGE resvexp:sneaker-1 0 -1 WITHSCORES
1) "c0a8f1de-5d3c-4b6e-9a53-7a4e2c1b9f10"
2) "1760100120123"
127.0.0.1:6379> HGETALL resv:sneaker-1:c0a8f1de-5d3c-4b6e-9a53-7a4e2c1b9f10
1) "user"
2) "u1"
3) "qty"
4) "1"
5) "status"
6) "RESERVED"
blocks.title: Walk one reservation through Redis

blocks.code:
$ curl -s -X POST \
    localhost:8080/api/sales/sneaker-1/reservations/c0a8f1de-5d3c-4b6e-9a53-7a4e2c1b9f10/confirm
{"status":"PAID"}
127.0.0.1:6379> XLEN stream:orders
(integer) 1
127.0.0.1:6379> XINFO GROUPS stream:orders
1) 1) "name"
   2) "fulfilment"
   3) "consumers"
   4) (integer) 1
   5) "pending"
   6) (integer) 0
   7) "last-delivered-id"
   8) "1760100005432-0"
   9) "entries-read"
  10) (integer) 1
  11) "lag"
  12) (integer) 0
127.0.0.1:6379> ZCARD resvexp:sneaker-1
(integer) 0
blocks.title: After the shopper pays

blocks.text:
`pending 0` and `lag 0` mean the worker has read and acknowledged everything. If the worker is stopped, new confirmations raise `lag`; if it reads but fails before `XACK`, they raise `pending`. Those two numbers are the first things to monitor on a stream pipeline.

### Tests: the oversell test

The test that matters is brutal and short: 500 distinct shoppers race for 100 units from 64 threads.

blocks.title: FlashSaleIT.java

blocks.text: Because the stream and sale keys persist inside one container for the whole test class, every test uses its own SKU (`race`, `idem`, `once`, `hold`, `order`) so tests do not disturb each other. The 500-way race uses distinct user ids on purpose; with a single user id the "one per shopper" rule would reject all but one request and the test would prove nothing about stock.

blocks.title: Watch out
blocks.text: `StringRedisTemplate.opsForStream().pending(...)` is shown here to assert the worker acknowledged everything; if your Spring Data Redis version names this method differently, `XPENDING` through a `RedisCallback` is an equally good check. Keep the assertion: a worker that processes but forgets `XACK` passes every other test and slowly fills the PEL in production.

### Demo: the thundering herd

With the service running, open a sale of 100 and let 2,000 requests from 100 different users hit it with 50 in parallel:

blocks.code:
$ curl -s -X POST "localhost:8080/api/sales/air-max?stock=100"
{"sku":"air-max","stock":100}
$ seq 1 2000 | xargs -P 50 -I{} sh -c \
    'curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" -X POST \
     localhost:8080/api/sales/air-max/reservations \
     -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d "{\"userId\":\"u{}\",\"qty\":1}"' | sort | uniq -c
    100 201
   1900 409
$ curl -s localhost:8080/api/sales/air-max
{"sku":"air-max","stock":0}
blocks.title: Oversell check from the outside

blocks.text: Exactly 100 `201` responses, no matter how often you repeat it. Now do the experiment that teaches the most: change `reserve.lua` into three separate Java calls (`GET`, compare, `DECRBY`) and run the demo again. You will see more than 100 successes and a negative stock. That is the oversell the script exists to prevent.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: How would you prevent overselling in a flash sale? Make the check and the decrement a single atomic operation. In Redis that is a Lua script (or `DECR` with a check of the returned value and compensation, which briefly shows negative stock). Avoid read-then-write from the application. Add reservation holds with a deadline so abandoned carts return stock, idempotency keys so retries do not double-spend, and treat Redis as the fast gate while the order database remains the system of record, reconciled from a durable stream.

blocks.title: Real world
blocks.text: Real sales add layers in front of this: a queue or waiting room that admits users at a controlled rate, bot protection, CDN caching of the product page so only the reserve call reaches Redis, and reconciliation jobs that compare Redis stock with the database. The atomic script at the centre looks very much like the one here.

### Extension ideas

- **Stable consumer identity plus** `XAUTOCLAIM`**.** Name consumers after the pod, and add a second scheduled task that calls `XAUTOCLAIM` for entries idle more than 60 seconds so a dead worker's backlog is adopted by a live one.
- **Dead-letter stream.** After N delivery attempts (see `XPENDING` delivery counts), move the entry to `stream:orders:dead` and alert.
- **Persist to a database.** Replace `OrderStore` with a JPA repository and a unique constraint on the order id; the constraint is the final idempotency guard.
- **Waiting room.** Add a sorted set of queued users and admit 200 per second into the reserve endpoint.
- **Reconciliation.** A nightly job compares `stock + reserved + paid` with the initial stock for every sale and alerts on drift.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
What this project proves:

- Atomic Lua scripts beat `WATCH` retries and locks for hot-counter workloads; design them check-first, write-last.
- Use one structure as the arbiter of state (here the expiry sorted set) so competing paths, confirm versus expire, cannot both win.
- Put idempotency inside the atomic step and make consumers idempotent as well; streams deliver at least once.
- Acknowledge after the work; watch `lag` and `pending` on every consumer group.
- Prove correctness with a concurrency test that would fail for the naive implementation.

sections.title: Project D: A Live Leaderboard with Notifications

blocks.text:
### Goal and requirements

ShopStream runs a daily "Shopper Rewards" challenge: every purchase earns points, and a live leaderboard shows the top shoppers. When someone enters the top 10 or takes the lead, they get a notification; everybody watching the page sees the board update without refreshing. This project combines four Redis features that usually appear separately: a sorted set for ranking, a stream as the durable event log, Pub/Sub for live fan-out, and a HyperLogLog for counting unique players.

rows: Sorted set `lb:points:daily:{date}`; `ZINCRBY` adds points, `ZREVRANGE` reads the top
`ZREVRANK` for "you are 7th", then a short range around that position
HyperLogLog `uv:players:{date}` with `PFADD` and `PFCOUNT`, about 12 KB per key at most
A worker in consumer group `notifier` reads the stream and publishes to Pub/Sub, acknowledging after publish
Pub/Sub channels `chan:board` (everyone) and `chan:notify:{player}` (one player), received by every service instance and pushed to browsers over Server-Sent Events (SSE)
One Lua script updates the board, the HyperLogLog and the stream and reports the old and new rank
blocks.caption: Requirements.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text: Why not push straight from the web request to the browsers? Because with two or more service instances, the instance that handles the purchase is rarely the one holding a given browser's SSE connection. Pub/Sub is the bus that reaches every instance. And why the stream in the middle? Pub/Sub is fire-and-forget: a message published while an instance is restarting is gone. The stream keeps every event until a consumer acknowledges it, so the forwarding step can retry.
### Architecture

blocks.code:
POST /api/points
      │
      ▼
ScoreService ── score.lua ──► lb:points:daily:{date}   ZINCRBY (+ old/new rank)
                         ├──► uv:players:{date}        PFADD
                         └──► stream:score-events      XADD MAXLEN ~ 10000
                                     │
                     group "notifier" │ XREADGROUP / XACK
                                     ▼
                             EventForwarder ──► PUBLISH chan:board
                                             └► PUBLISH chan:notify:{player}  (rank events)
                                                       │
       every instance subscribes (PSUBSCRIBE chan:*)  ▼
                             RedisMessageListenerContainer ──► SseHub ──► browsers (EventSource)

blocks.text: ### Project layout

blocks.code:
leaderboard/
├── pom.xml                       (as Project A, web + data-redis + actuator + test)
├── docker-compose.yml            (same Redis service)
└── src
    ├── main
    │   ├── java/com/shopstream/leaderboard
    │   │   ├── LeaderboardApplication.java
    │   │   ├── ScoreService.java
    │   │   ├── EventForwarder.java
    │   │   ├── PubSubConfig.java
    │   │   ├── SseHub.java
    │   │   └── LeaderboardController.java
    │   └── resources
    │       ├── application.yml
    │       ├── scripts/score.lua
    │       └── static/index.html
    └── test/java/com/shopstream/leaderboard
        ├── RedisTestConfig.java
        └── LeaderboardIT.java

blocks.text: The Redis keys of this project:

rows: Player to points for one day, expires after 8 days
Approximate count of distinct players who scored that day
Every scoring event, trimmed to about 10,000 entries
Live board updates for all viewers
blocks.caption: Keys.

blocks.text:
### The scoring script

Two things need atomicity: the old rank must be read before the increment and the new rank after it, with no other score change in between, and the three structures must be updated together.

blocks.code:
-- KEYS: 1 daily leaderboard, 2 unique-players HLL, 3 event stream
-- ARGV: 1 player id, 2 points to add, 3 board TTL in seconds
-- Returns { new score (string), old rank (0-based, -1 if new), new rank (0-based) }
local oldRank = redis.call('ZREVRANK', KEYS[1], ARGV[1])
local score = redis.call('ZINCRBY', KEYS[1], ARGV[2], ARGV[1])
local newRank = redis.call('ZREVRANK', KEYS[1], ARGV[1])
redis.call('EXPIRE', KEYS[1], tonumber(ARGV[3]))
redis.call('PFADD', KEYS[2], ARGV[1])
redis.call('EXPIRE', KEYS[2], tonumber(ARGV[3]))

local old = -1
if oldRank then
  old = oldRank
end
redis.call('XADD', KEYS[3], 'MAXLEN', '~', '10000', '*',
           'player', ARGV[1], 'points', ARGV[2], 'score', score,
           'oldRank', tostring(old), 'newRank', tostring(newRank))
return { score, old, newRank }
blocks.title: scripts/score.lua

blocks.text: What to notice: `ZREVRANK` returns a nil reply for a player not in the set, which a Lua script sees as `false`, so we convert it to `-1`. Ranks are 0-based in Redis; the Java side adds one for humans. `XADD ... MAXLEN ~ 10000` trims approximately, which is cheaper than exact trimming: Redis removes whole internal blocks, so the stream may hold a little more than 10,000 entries.

blocks.title: Gotcha
blocks.text: Sorted sets order players with equal scores by member name (lexicographically). If "fairness" matters, the player who reached 500 points first should rank higher. A common trick encodes the time in the fractional part of the score, for example `points + (1 - timestamp / 1e13)`. Doubles hold about 15 to 16 significant digits, so check that your points and timestamps fit before you try it.
### The score service

blocks.title: ScoreService.java

blocks.text:
What to notice: the sorted set operations cost `O(log N)` for the rank and `O(log N + M)` for a range of `M` entries, so a board with 10 million players answers "top 10" and "my rank" in microseconds to low milliseconds on the server. The `Set` returned by `reverseRangeWithScores` is a `LinkedHashSet`, so iteration order is Redis order; if you ever copy it into a `HashSet` the order is lost.

### From stream to Pub/Sub

The forwarder is a consumer-group worker, structured exactly like the order worker in the flash-sale project: pending entries first, then new ones, acknowledge after the work. The "work" here is publishing.

blocks.title: EventForwarder.java

blocks.text: If the process dies after `convertAndSend` but before `acknowledge`, the entry is delivered again and viewers see a duplicate board update. For a leaderboard that is harmless (the board message carries the absolute score and rank, not a delta). Notifications are more sensitive; if duplicates would annoy users, record "notified:{player}:{date}" with `SET` `NX` before sending.

blocks.title: Watch out
blocks.text: `Pub/Sub` delivers only to currently connected subscribers and does not buffer. If nobody is subscribed, `PUBLISH` returns `0` and the message is gone. That is why the durable record is the stream and why a browser that reconnects must reload `GET /api/leaderboard` to resynchronise instead of expecting missed events.

### Receiving messages and pushing to browsers

Spring Boot does not create a `RedisMessageListenerContainer` for you. Declare one, subscribe with a pattern, and hand every message to the hub that owns the SSE connections.

blocks.title: PubSubConfig.java
SseHub.java

blocks.text:
What to notice:

- **One pattern subscription, two kinds of channel.** `PSUBSCRIBE chan:*` receives `chan:board` and every `chan:notify:{player}`. Pattern subscriptions are convenient; with hundreds of thousands of personal channels you may prefer to subscribe per connected player instead, so Redis does less matching.
- **The container uses its own connection.** A connection in subscribe mode can run no other commands, so the container holds a dedicated one and delivers messages on a task executor thread. Your normal template calls use other connections.
- **The hub is local state.** A connection to instance A is only known to A. This is why every instance must subscribe: each instance forwards the Pub/Sub message to its own browsers.
- **Cleanup on every exit path.** Without `onCompletion`, `onTimeout` and `onError`, closed browsers leak emitters forever, and each broadcast then throws on dead connections.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text: `HyperLogLog` trades accuracy for size. `PFCOUNT` has a standard error of about 0.81 percent, and the structure never exceeds roughly 12 KB per key regardless of how many players it has seen. For a few players the estimate is exact, which is why the sample shows 3. If you need the exact set of distinct ids, use a `SET`, and pay memory proportional to the number of players.

### Tests

The test class reuses the `RedisTestConfig` container bean from the earlier projects. The SSE test opens a real HTTP connection, waits for the greeting, posts points over HTTP, and waits for the push.

blocks.title: LeaderboardIT.java

blocks.text: The SSE test crosses every layer: the HTTP post, the Lua script, the stream, the scheduled forwarder, `PUBLISH`, the listener container, the hub and the HTTP response. It is slower than the others (about 100 ms of polling latency) but it is the one that fails when you misspell a channel name or forget `@EnableScheduling`.

blocks.title: Watch out
blocks.text: The notification assertion depends on `sse-dana` being the first player on a fresh board when the test runs, or at least entering the top 10. With 9,000 points she takes the lead on any board the other tests have built, because they award at most a few hundred points; if you add tests with larger awards, give this one more points or a separate Redis database.

blocks.title: Cross-instance push

blocks.text: The purchase went to port 8081, a forwarder in one of the two instances published it, and the SSE connection on port 8082 received the push. If both instances run the forwarder, the consumer group makes sure each stream entry is forwarded by exactly one of them (barring a crash), so viewers do not see duplicates in normal operation.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: When would you use Pub/Sub, and when a stream, for notifications? Pub/Sub is for live fan-out where losing a message while nobody is listening is acceptable (a UI update, a cache-invalidation hint). A stream is for events you must not lose: it persists entries, supports consumer groups with acknowledgements, and lets a crashed consumer resume. Production designs often use both: the stream as the durable log and a forwarder that republishes to Pub/Sub for the low-latency, many-listener part.

blocks.title: Real world
blocks.text: Leaderboards in games and apps are one of the best-known uses of sorted sets because `ZADD`/`ZINCRBY` and rank queries are logarithmic. At very large scale teams shard boards (by region, season or score bucket) and keep an approximate global rank; the principle, one sorted set per board and a stream as the audit log, stays the same.

### Extension ideas

- **Weekly and all-time boards.** Add `ZUNIONSTORE` with the last 7 daily boards into `lb:points:weekly`, cached for a minute, and compare its cost with an incrementally maintained weekly board.
- **Last-Event-ID replay.** Put the stream entry id into the SSE `id:` field. On reconnect the browser sends `Last-Event-ID`; read the missed entries with `XRANGE` and replay them.
- **Per-player channels on demand.** Subscribe to `chan:notify:{player}` only when a player connects, with `RedisMessageListenerContainer.addMessageListener` and `removeMessageListener`.
- **Sharded Pub/Sub.** Replace `PUBLISH` with `SPUBLISH` and `SSUBSCRIBE` to scale Pub/Sub on a Redis Cluster.
- **Tie-break by time.** Implement the fractional-score trick and write a test showing that two players with equal points rank by who got there first.
- **Backpressure.** Limit each SSE connection to one event per 250 ms by coalescing board updates in the hub.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
What this project proves:

- A sorted set gives you ranking, rank lookup and neighbour queries with logarithmic cost; `ZINCRBY` is the scoring primitive.
- Run several related updates in one Lua script when they must agree, here the board, the HyperLogLog and the event log.
- Combine a stream (durable, acknowledged) with Pub/Sub (instant, lossy) instead of choosing one; every instance subscribes, each browser connects to just one.
- Clients must resynchronise after a reconnect because Pub/Sub does not replay.
- HyperLogLog counts distinct items in a small fixed size with a small, known error.
